title: Getting started
text:
While the RAP Development team won’t be able to work closely with all teams right away, there are steps teams should take to get started on RAP development.

Develop process maps for each analytical output. These will be useful to help understand existing SAS processes, highlight areas for improvement and plan RAP development work. We have written guidance and produced an example map to help you get started.
Consider R training needs in your team.

Contact the NRS Learning & Development team to find out about upcoming training courses on offer in NRS.
Review the Scottish Government R training on offer and keep an eye on the OCS newsletter for other opportunities.

Consider whether there are any technical barriers to your team using the current R environment on NRScotland (e.g. data access, memory constraints) and raise these with the RAP Development team.
Think about other planned or potential changes to your analysis and how this might impact RAP development. For example, consider proposed changes of the publication review work.
Follow coding good practices when writing R code. We will develop more thorough guidance for NRS soon, but this is a good place to start.
Attend RAP Show and Tidy sessions to learn from others and consider presenting your own development work (no matter how big or small!)
Familiarise yourself with existing RAP resources:

Government Analysis Function RAP Guidance
RAP Self Assessment Tool
Quality Assurance of Code for Analysis and Research (Duck Book)

title: Why RAP?
text:
Reproducible Analytical Pipelines (RAPs) are analytical processes that have been developed in a way that promotes reproducibility, efficiency and quality.
Some common examples of a RAP approach in practice are:

Using open-source software (e.g. R or Python) over proprietary software (e.g. SAS)
Automating tasks where possible to minimise manual steps
Using version control software (e.g. Git) to create an audit trail of changes
Good documentation stored in the same place as the code
Regular peer review of code to improve quality and shared understanding
Built in quality assurance to give early indication of problems

These are just some examples, however there are many more that could be applied depending on the requirements of the project.
It is important to note that RAP is not all or nothing, or once and done. You do not need to apply all possible RAP principles to achieve benefits, and improvements should be an ongoing process. Adopting a RAP approach will involve some quick wins, some up-front investment for bigger long-term gains, and continuous improvement.
You can read more about RAP and examples of good practice on the Government Analysis Function website.
Embedding a RAP approach in NRS will help us to:

Transition from SAS to Open Source software
Improve efficiency of processes to free up time for other work
Ensure processes are well understood, easy to maintain and robust to staff changes

Teams may already be following some RAP principles in existing SAS processes. However, transitioning from SAS to open-source software will offer further opportunities to strengthen this approach and realise more benefits.

title: Using Git
text: Git is an open source version control tool. It integrates with GitHub or Azure DevOps to allowing you to maintain clear versions of all coding projects.

title: Using Git
text:
Explaining the Jargon
All version control tools come with a set of jargon. In this section we aim to break down what each of those terms mean and how they apply to using git within GitHub or Azure DevOps.

Repository or Repo
This is the storage location of the project files along with the log of the complete history of changes made to the project files. For all projects you will encounter two main repositories.
Local - The local repository, sometimes referenced to as the Working directory refers to the project directory stored on the working machine. Such as within shared file storage, network drive or laptops C: drive. It is the directory in which you will be working and saving your files.
Remote - The remote repository is hosted on platforms such as GitHub or Azure DevOps. It is primarily used for backup and collaboration. It is usually what is known as a bare directory containing git files, history and metadata but not working files.
Git is used to facilitate communication between these two levels of repository. If the local repository already exists you can initialize the remote repository using the command line prompt:
git init
If the remote repository has already been initiated you can create a local copy by using the command prompt:
git clone
For more information on project structure refer to page:


Guide to Devops



Branches
Every new repository will be created with an origin branch know as main or master. This branch should be used to store the final or stable, ready for use, version of the code.
Therefore it is good coding practice to develop code on a working branch. This is particularly good practice when working in teams as it allows every team member to work within their own branch and reduces risk of overwriting stable code and introducing bugs and errors to the main code line while they are developing. Once development is concluded the branch can be merged into the main stable codebase. Branches can also be used to test fixes for bugs.
To create a new branch locally and move into that branch you can run the command:
git checkout -b <name>
You will then need to link your local branch to the remote branch using the command:
git push --set-upstream origin <name>
A new branch can also be created within your version control tool (GitHub, DevOps) and then
git checkout <name>
For more information on dealing with bug fixes, pull requests and code merging within DevOps:

Guide to DevOps - Pull requests



Three Data States



Figure of Git’s three main sections


There are three main states any file can exist within:
modified - files that have been add, removed or edited within the working directory.
staged - selected changes are temporarily recorded or indexed before they are committed to the git directory which stores the metadata and objects associated with the modifications that have been staged. To stage files you use the command:
git add
committed - committing takes files recorded in the staging area and stores a snapshot permanently within the git directory. Each commit is assigned a hash code that allows you to access the snapshot. Therefore if you want to roll-back to a particular snapshot you can access it via its hash code. Staged files can be committed as follows:
`git commit -m “message”
A commit message is also added to all commit commands. This is to add context to the update within the git directory. A good commit message should be short and succinct but also give clear messaging about what you have changed. For example if you were fixing a bug, in a function called Check_file that was identified in pull request number 33 your commit message may look like:
git commit -m "!33: bug fix in Check_file - Solved"
The above commit message clearly states it is working on issue/pull request number 33 in which a bug was identified in the function Check_file and that it has been tested and marked as solved ready for merging.






Important



Remember to push


All of these are within the local repository. In order to back up the committed changes you have to push your changes to the remote repository. This can be done using the command:
git push
If you do not push your commits they will not be recorded in your remote repository and will not be backed up or be available to be accessed by collaborators.


Command line quick reference
# Initialize a remote repository from local folder
git init

# Clone a repository from remote
git clone

# To update local files to match remote repository
git pull

# To create a new local branch 
git checkout -b <name>

# Move onto a branch 
git checkout <name>

# Link a locale branch to the remote branch
git push --set-upstream origin <name>

# Link a local branch to the remote branch
git push --set-upstream origin name

# To stage all modified files
git add .

# To stage a single file
git add <file>

# To commit files to local repository
git commit -m "message"

# To push changes to remote repository
git push

# Check status of files
git status

title: Using Git
text:
Git within R studio
In order to use git within RStudio you must have the directory set up as an R project. Therefore any cloned repository must contain a Rproj file.
You can use all of the above command lined within the terminal window of RStudio, however RStudio also offers a graphical interface that some may find preferable to use. To access open the Tools menu and access Version Control menu and Commit.... You can also access this with the keyboard short cut Ctrl+Alt+M.



Menu access to version control tools within R Studio


Within the commit screen you can easily change branch, overview any documents modified (M), added (A) or removed (R) and investigate those changes when compared to the remote branch. Changes can be staged by ticking the box within the stage column. A commit message can be added and changes committed to the local branch. Then changes can be pushed to the remote branch.



Version control tools within R studio

title: Process Mapping
text: This document introduces process mapping and explains why it is a useful tool for documenting and improving analytical processes. Process maps provide a clear, visual overview of how data flows from inputs through processing and analysis to final outputs. They support transparency, shared understanding, and more efficient ways of working. They can also support work within existing SAS projects, help teams track and document their analytical pipeline, and provide a clear foundation when transitioning to open‑source tools.

title: Process Mapping
text:
What is a process map?
A process map is a method for documenting and visualising the steps required to move from the beginning to the end of a process. In the context of NRS statistics, a process may relate to the production of publications, management information, data tables, or any other analytical work that is carried out on a recurring basis.
Process maps can vary in their level of detail; however, it is generally helpful to include the following key elements:

Input data: These may come from a database, a flat file, or be manually defined within code.
Manual steps: These can include tasks such as copying and pasting data between files, renaming or moving files, or carrying out manual quality assurance checks.
Code or programs: These may consist of SAS programs, R scripts, or other automated processing tools. In some cases, it may also be useful to include details of the main tasks the code carries out.
Outputs: These can include data files, charts saved as image files, formatted Excel spreadsheets, publication reports, or dashboards.

title: Process Mapping
text:
Why create a process map?
A process map is an invaluable piece of documentation for any analytical process. It can help you to:

Develop a shared understanding within your team of what the process involves. This is particularly useful for managers or others who are not closely involved in the day-to-day technical delivery.
Explain the process to others, such as a new team member or a colleague from the RAP Development team who may be supporting redevelopment work.
Spot opportunities to improve the process, such as areas where steps could be simplified, reordered, or combined.
Make it easier to develop the process in a non‑linear way, for example by showing where improving outputs or visualisations first could be more useful than starting at the beginning.

Even if a process has already undergone redevelopment, creating a process map remains valuable, particularly for building shared understanding and supporting knowledge transfer. In addition, further opportunities for improvement may still be uncovered.

title: Process Mapping
section: Top tips for creating a process map
text:
Top tips for creating a process map

Start simple. Begin with a high-level view of the process. If it becomes clear that additional detail is needed, this can always be added later.
Don’t worry about using specialist software. Simple text boxes and arrows in PowerPoint or Word are often sufficient. Tools like Microsoft Visio can also work well, but they are not essential.
Use symbols consistently. Use different symbols to distinguish between data, code, and manual steps.
Have a clear key or legend to explain what each symbol represents. The specific symbols you choose are less important than using them consistently.
Keep the scope manageable. Avoid trying to capture multiple processes, or an overly large process, in a single map. A good rule of thumb is to create one map per publication or equivalent analytical product. If a map becomes too large or complex, consider splitting it into separate maps, for example, one for data processing and another for producing outputs.
Keep your process map with your code where possible. It makes it easier to find later. This also follows RAP principles by keeping documentation alongside the code base, rather than in a separate location. If it is not possible to store the process map with the code, it should be kept alongside the rest of the project documentation.
You don’t need to understand every line of your code to produce a useful process map. It is about capturing the flow, not the detail.

title: Process Mapping
text:
Example process map
The example process map below is based on NHSCR, which is a SAS process run on monthly and quarterly basis. It reads in multiple datasets, applies a series of transformations, and produces a set of output data files. This example focuses on illustrating a section of that flow.

This process map uses different symbols to represent input files, data manipulation, intermediate files, and outputs. Using consistent symbols keeps the map clear and easy to follow, and helps readers quickly understand the flow of data through the process.
Looking at the map also helps illustrate some of the practical benefits of process mapping in action. For example:

It allows someone new to the process, or unfamiliar with the code, to quickly see which data files are required and what outputs are produced.
It highlights where similar steps are repeated across multiple process flows, which can prompt discussion about whether parts of the process could be simplified or reused to reduce repetition.

title: Process Mapping
text:
Using Microsoft Visio
Microsoft Visio is a useful tool for creating process maps within NRS, as it is available through Microsoft 365. When you open Visio, you can choose from a range of templates, including a basic diagram or a standard flowchart template with commonly used symbols.
When creating process maps, the priority should be to get started rather than focusing on unnecessary complexity. Using simple, clear shapes and flows with keys will help ensure that your process map is easy to follow.
Visio files can be saved in visio file format (.vsdx), which allows you to revisit and edit them later. You can also export them as images (.png) or PDF files. However, exported versions cannot be edited, so make sure to keep the original Visio file for any future updates.
For more guidance on using Visio, please refer to these slides on building process maps.

title: Differences Between SAS and R
text:
Translating SAS code to R (and other coding languages, such as Python) can introduce subtle - and sometimes serious - risks. These arise because the languages differ in defaults, data structures, numerical handling, and modelling assumptions. This guidance aims to provide an overview of some of the risk areas to watch out for, and how to mitigate them.
SAS performs many actions automatically that are not obvious from the source code. These behaviours can be easy to miss when translating to R and may only become apparent when outputs are compared.
For this reason, translated code should always be validated against known SAS outputs wherever possible.

title: Differences Between SAS and R
text:
Implicit SAS engine behaviour
One of the most important translation risks is behaviour that is provided by the SAS engine rather than explicitly written in the code.
Examples include:

Missing values being silently dropped from arithmetic calculations.
Automatic warnings when values exceed a declared LENGTH.
Sort-dependent BY-group behaviour.
MERGE behaviour when datasets differ in length.
Type conversion warnings.

Because these behaviours are not always visible in the source code, they are particularly easy for translators and AI-assisted conversion tools to miss. A script can run successfully in R while still producing different results from the original SAS program.






Note



Validation against known outputs, combined with awareness of implicit SAS behaviour, is essential.

title: Differences Between SAS and R
text:
Character case sensitivity
R is fully case-sensitive whereas SAS language keywords and many programming constructs are not. For example, in R
Age
and
age
are different variables. This may cause translation errors.

title: Differences Between SAS and R
text:
Rounding
SAS uses the rounding rule “round half away from zero”.
round(2.5)   /* 3 */
Base R uses “round half to even”, also known as bankers rounding.
round(2.5)   # 2
The function round_half_up() from the janitor package can be used in R to apply the rounding rule “round half away from zero” when consistency with SAS or Excel is required.
library(janitor)
round_half_up(2.5)   # 3

title: Differences Between SAS and R
text:
Missing values
In SAS, many summary functions automatically ignore missing values.
mean(10, ., 20)     /* 15 */

sum(10, ., 20)      /* 30 */
In R, missing values propagate by default. Entire outputs may become NA if missing values are not handled explicitly.
mean(c(10, NA, 20)) # NA  

sum(c(10, NA, 20)) # NA
To reproduce SAS behaviour:
mean(c(10, NA, 20), na.rm = TRUE) # 15
sum(c(10, NA, 20), na.rm = TRUE) # 30

title: Differences Between SAS and R
Differences Between SAS and R
text:
Substring extraction
In SAS, substr(x, y, z) means for string x, start at position y and return z characters.
substr("1234567", 3, 4)    /* "3456" */
In R, substr(x, y, z) means for string x, start at position y and stop at position z.
substr("1234567", 3, 4) # "34"
To replicate SAS behaviour:
substr("1234567", 3, 6) # "3456"

title: Differences Between SAS and R
text:
Dates
SAS stores dates as the number of days since 1 January 1960, whereas R stores dates as the number of days since 1 January 1970. Direct comparison of raw date values without conversion will produce incorrect results.

title: Differences Between SAS and R
Differences Between SAS and R
text:
Merging datasets
SAS MERGE is not equivalent to any R join and can produce unexpected results if datasets contain different numbers of observations within a BY group.
data merged;

  merge a b;

  by id;

run;
When translating SAS code, it is important to understand the intended relationship between the datasets:

One-to-one
One-to-many
Many-to-one
Many-to-many

In R, joins are usually implemented using functions such as:
left_join(a, b, by = "id")

inner_join(a, b, by = "id")

full_join(a, b, by = "id")
Before translating a merge, verify the uniqueness of key variables and compare record counts before and after the join.

title: Differences Between SAS and R
text:
Type conversion
SAS frequently performs automatic type conversion between character and numeric variables and generates warnings when conversions occur.
x = "123";

y = x + 1;   /* 124 */
In R, character and numeric data types are generally more strictly separated.
x <- "123"

y <- x + 1   # Error in x + 1 : non-numeric argument to binary operator
When translating code, always check whether the original SAS program relies on implicit conversions. Failure to replicate these conversions may cause errors or unexpected missing values.
x <- "123" 

y <- as.numeric(x) + 1   # 124

title: Differences Between SAS and R
text:
Numeric precision
Although SAS and R both use double-precision arithmetic, calculations may not always produce exactly identical results.
Differences can arise from:

Statistical algorithm implementations
Optimisation routines
Numerical tolerances
Output formatting and rounding

For example, model parameter estimates may differ slightly while remaining statistically equivalent.
Validation should therefore focus on acceptable tolerances rather than requiring exact numerical equality for every value.

title: Differences Between SAS and R
text:
Logical values
SAS represents Boolean values numerically.
age > 18 /* 1 or 0 */
R uses a dedicated logical type.
age = 5
age > 18  # FALSE
age > 3   # TRUE

title: Differences Between SAS and R
text:
Validation and comparison
Code conversion should always be treated as a software validation exercise rather than a simple translation task.
Recommended checks include:

Record counts before and after major processing steps.
Frequency tables for key categorical variables.
Summary statistics for continuous variables.
Comparison of intermediate datasets, not only final outputs.
Independent review of translated code.
Tolerance-based comparison for numerical results.

Where possible, compare outputs against known SAS results rather than assuming that successfully executed R code is correct.






Note



When translating SAS code, assume that every result depends on three things: the written code, the structure of the data, and SAS behaviours that may not be explicitly visible. Successful translation requires validation of all three.

title: Using Azure Devops
text:
Azure DevOps opens at the Collections landing page. Each collection you have access to will appear on the left hand side of the screen.
Inside each collection is a Dashboard which gives access to the Projects within that collection (displayed as project cards), your assigned work items and any pull requests you have made or have been assigned to as a reviewer.



Collections landing page in Azure DevOps









Project side bar



When opening a project you will find a side bar with several options and tools.
For most projects only the Overview panel, Boards and Repos tools will be relevant, and they are explored in more detail below.
The remaining three panels facilitate the continuous integration, continuous delivery (CI/CD) software development. Therefore, the Pipelines, Test Plans and Artifacts tabs are not discussed in this training document.
[!IMPORTANT] The Pipeline and Testing panels are not to be confused with Reproducible Analytical Pipelines (RAPs). Instead they are used for production guidance and external stress-testing of the software before deployment.


The Overview panel aims to provide quick access to top level information about the project. This is where you can add a summary of the project and view team members. The general activity within the project will also be listed within the Summary section.



This panel is for project planning, team and task management, management of bug fixes and pull requests. Each board is categorised into a number of work items. These separate tasks by specific elements to aid in organisation within a team. The work items are as follows:


Work items or tickets are used to break down required tasks within a project. You can use these tags to highlight, assign and keep track of tasks, project progress and current thinking to help with cooperation across the project.
The tags can be broken down into different categories:
Bug - An error found within the code that causes it not to produce the intended consequences. These can range from minor issues, such as typos or small visual discrepancies, to more serious problems like incorrect functionality or potential security vulnerabilities. This tag can be sued to highlight known issues that are queued to be fixed.
Epic - Denotes a piece of work that is of High Importance. Usually, a large-scale element of the project that gives a broad overview. An Epic work item can be broken down into Features and User stories.



Example of Epic tag


This tag can be used to highlight the overarching steps on a process map or goals that a developer team may have.
Feature - Describes the development of functional pieces of work. The following example shows three Feature work items that may be part of the Epic tag above.


Task - This tag can be used to break down any of the other tags into actionable items. A to-do list of tasks can be created at the feature and Epic levels to help break down and assign workload between colleagues.

Test Case - This is a step-by-step guide breaking down the testing of the Project Features. This allows for the testers to continually check the functionality of the code and how it performs alongside the elements set out in the Epic and User Story tags.

User Story - Describes the build from the perspective of the user and how they would use and implement the code. This helps you think about the end user when developing the code, asking questions on how they would interact with the code and its outcomes.



Example of a user story tag










Repos menu



Within the Repos tab you can manage your code base, through tracking commits, pushes and pull requests. It is the viewing portal for the remote repository of the version control infrastructure. These features communicate with your Integrated Development Environment (IDE), an example of which is RStudio, where the development and testing of the code will be done, via Git. Git is an open source version control tool that allows you to maintain clear and backed up versions of all coding projects. More information on using Git within the R environment can be found on the page [Using Git in R]()






Files tab menu



You can open and view all files pushed to your remote repository within the Files tab. You can also find links for cloning and/or forking the repository. For each file, you can view its contents in the Contents pane located at the top.
The History pane shows the history of changes made to the file, listing the associated commit, the type of change and any associated pull requests. You can directly access the Compare pane for a specific commit from the history table or from within the Compare tab. You can select which commits you want to compare. The changes can either be viewed side by side or in-line.
The final pane is the Blame pane. This highlights which bits of the code have been edited, when they were pushed to the repository and by which team member.






Note



Blame is not a negative term within software development instead it records and displays the author of specific lines in a file, allowing for collaboration and integration within a team.









Example of a commit graph



The Commits tab shows a list of all commits made to the repository and also presents them in a visual format known as a commit graph. This makes it easy to explore the project’s branches, commits, and merges in a clear, graphical way.
The tab also allows you to filter the commits by author, date and status. Once you have located a commit of interest you can explore and compare the changes made in the commit. You can also make comments, branch from or roll back to that commit.



Similar to the Commits tab, the Pushes tab allows you to explore the pushes made to the repository and the commits within those pushes.
More information in the difference between commits and pushes can be found on the page [Using Git in R]() in the Understanding the Jargon section.



Branches provide isolated environments for developing and testing changes independently. Changes can be made to the code and ideas can be tested without affecting the main project. Branches enable multiple team members to work on the codebase simultaneously without affecting the existing code.
From the Branches tab you can observe which branches are operational, which branches may have been merged into the codebase, or those that may have been abandoned (known as stale branches). You can also see how many commits a branch is ahead or behind the main branch, along with any pull requests associated with the branch. New remote branches can also be created from this tab. Once a new remote branch has been created you will need to ’checkout` to the branch within the local repository. For information on navigating branches in Git see the page [Using Git in R]()
It is good coding practice to work within a branch, even if you are a single developer. It separates working code from developmental code which in turn allows for ease of roll backs. Further information on good coding practices can be found in the guidance page - [Coding Standards page]()



Pull requests are a collaborative tool allowing you to submit proposed changes to the overall code base. They are an essential part of good coding practice, especially when working on ongoing projects or within a team. Before a piece of work can be moved from a branch to the main code, it must first go through a code review process. This is where peers will review the code, and is an opportunity to spot any typos, regions where code can be made more efficient, or tidied to match the group coding style. Once you have completed work within a branch on the repository you can create a pull request from either inside the branch or via the pull request tab.



Example of pull request


Within the pull request screen you can assign reviewers, both required and optional. As the virtual machine is not connected to the internet, it will not automatically notify reviewers. Any assigned reviewers will have to be notified manually. Comments and discussions of the work can also be made within the overview or within individual files. Once all changes have been made and approved the branch can then be merged with the main branch from inside the pull request.
For more information on pull requests you can find more information on both making and responding to pull requests in both GitHub and Azure DevOps within the [Working with Pull request]() page.

Task - This tag can be used to break down any of the other tags into actionable items. A to-do list of tasks can be created at the feature and Epic levels to help break down and assign workload between colleagues.

Test Case - This is a step-by-step guide breaking down the testing of the Project Features. This allows for the testers to continually check the functionality of the code and how it performs alongside the elements set out in the Epic and User Story tags.

User Story - Describes the build from the perspective of the user and how they would use and implement the code. This helps you think about the end user when developing the code, asking questions on how they would interact with the code and its outcomes.



Example of a user story tag










Repos menu



Within the Repos tab you can manage your code base, through tracking commits, pushes and pull requests. It is the viewing portal for the remote repository of the version control infrastructure. These features communicate with your Integrated Development Environment (IDE), an example of which is RStudio, where the development and testing of the code will be done, via Git. Git is an open source version control tool that allows you to maintain clear and backed up versions of all coding projects. More information on using Git within the R environment can be found on the page [Using Git in R]()






Files tab menu



You can open and view all files pushed to your remote repository within the Files tab. You can also find links for cloning and/or forking the repository. For each file, you can view its contents in the Contents pane located at the top.
The History pane shows the history of changes made to the file, listing the associated commit, the type of change and any associated pull requests. You can directly access the Compare pane for a specific commit from the history table or from within the Compare tab. You can select which commits you want to compare. The changes can either be viewed side by side or in-line.
The final pane is the Blame pane. This highlights which bits of the code have been edited, when they were pushed to the repository and by which team member.






Note



Blame is not a negative term within software development instead it records and displays the author of specific lines in a file, allowing for collaboration and integration within a team.









Example of a commit graph



The Commits tab shows a list of all commits made to the repository and also presents them in a visual format known as a commit graph. This makes it easy to explore the project’s branches, commits, and merges in a clear, graphical way.
The tab also allows you to filter the commits by author, date and status. Once you have located a commit of interest you can explore and compare the changes made in the commit. You can also make comments, branch from or roll back to that commit.



Similar to the Commits tab, the Pushes tab allows you to explore the pushes made to the repository and the commits within those pushes.
More information in the difference between commits and pushes can be found on the page [Using Git in R]() in the Understanding the Jargon section.



Branches provide isolated environments for developing and testing changes independently. Changes can be made to the code and ideas can be tested without affecting the main project. Branches enable multiple team members to work on the codebase simultaneously without affecting the existing code.
From the Branches tab you can observe which branches are operational, which branches may have been merged into the codebase, or those that may have been abandoned (known as stale branches). You can also see how many commits a branch is ahead or behind the main branch, along with any pull requests associated with the branch. New remote branches can also be created from this tab. Once a new remote branch has been created you will need to ’checkout` to the branch within the local repository. For information on navigating branches in Git see the page [Using Git in R]()
It is good coding practice to work within a branch, even if you are a single developer. It separates working code from developmental code which in turn allows for ease of roll backs. Further information on good coding practices can be found in the guidance page - [Coding Standards page]()



Pull requests are a collaborative tool allowing you to submit proposed changes to the overall code base. They are an essential part of good coding practice, especially when working on ongoing projects or within a team. Before a piece of work can be moved from a branch to the main code, it must first go through a code review process. This is where peers will review the code, and is an opportunity to spot any typos, regions where code can be made more efficient, or tidied to match the group coding style. Once you have completed work within a branch on the repository you can create a pull request from either inside the branch or via the pull request tab.



Example of pull request


Within the pull request screen you can assign reviewers, both required and optional. As the virtual machine is not connected to the internet, it will not automatically notify reviewers. Any assigned reviewers will have to be notified manually. Comments and discussions of the work can also be made within the overview or within individual files. Once all changes have been made and approved the branch can then be merged with the main branch from inside the pull request.
For more information on pull requests you can find more information on both making and responding to pull requests in both GitHub and Azure DevOps within the [Working with Pull request]() page.

title: NRS RAP Book
text:
This book contains information on developing Reproducible Analytical Pipelines (RAPs) in National Records of Scotland (NRS).
The content has been developed by the RAP Development team, who joined NRS in 2026. The team’s role is to lead the implementation of RAP across statistics and analysis production in NRS.
Please get in touch with the RAP Development team if you have any feedback or questions.

title: Working with the RAP Development team
text: Our goal in NRS is for RAP to be the default approach to analysis. To achieve this goal, we will:

title: Working with the RAP Development team
text:
Defining our RAP approach
To succeed in our goal, it is important we all have a shared understanding of what RAP is and what we mean by a ‘RAP approach’. We will do this by:

Running awareness sessions for all statisticians and managers
Sharing clear guidance, both technical and non-technical
Developing tools for use across teams to promote consistency

title: Working with the RAP Development team
text:
Project support
Different teams and projects will require different levels of involvement from the RAP Development team. Support might look like this:

A RAP developer is embedded in a team to lead the planning and development of a RAP for a specific project. They train the statistics team to apply RAP principles and co-develop code to meet agreed standards.
RAP development is led by the statistics team with guidance from the RAP Development team through regular meetings and code review.
The statistics team engages with the RAP community, follows NRS guidance and contacts RAP Development team for ad-hoc support and advice when required.

Our level of involvement and timing of when support is offered will vary from team to team depending on the following factors:








Factor
Light Support
Embedded Support




R & RAP skills
Strong skills
New to R


Time available for development
Adequate time
Limited time


Overall SAS workload
Small
Large


Previous support from RAP Development team
Already supported
No prior support



We will arrange a session with each statistics team to discuss these factors, their current preparedness for RAP, plans for development, and support needs. By collecting this information from each team, we can begin to make a plan for the order we will work with teams, and what level of involvement will be most suitable.

title: Working with the RAP Development team
text:
Planned projects
The following projects have been identified as priorities for the RAP Development team:

NHSCR Monthly Extract: As there are currently no statisticians working in the NHSCR team, the RAP Development team have adopted their monthly extract SAS process as our first project. This will give us, as a team, the chance to develop our understanding of NRS systems and software, record our learnings, and once complete, present this as a case study of RAP best practice for other teams to learn from.
Vital Events project TBD: The Vital Events team have a large number of resource-intensive SAS processes. Therefore, we plan to engage with this team early to identify a project that will help develop skills and free up time for further development work.
